title: Why Port Cranes Move in That Strange Hesitant Rhythm
hook: Why does this crane keep slowing down for no reason?
loop: Ends on 'which is why, at every container port on earth,' handing back into scene 2. Pattern A.

scenes.text: A container crane never moves at a steady speed. It rushes, eases, then creeps the last few metres.
Over and over, on every lift.
So is the operator being careful? Feeling their way into position by eye?
Not at all. Most of that motion is not a choice.
A container hanging from cables is a pendulum. One that weighs thirty tons.
And a pendulum has a natural rhythm set only by the length of its cables.
On a tall port crane, one full swing takes around eight seconds.
Start the trolley moving, and the container is left behind, then swings forward past it.
Stop the trolley, and the container keeps going.
A swinging thirty ton box cannot be placed into a slot with centimetres of clearance.
So the crane does something counterintuitive. It starts a second swing on purpose.
It accelerates, pauses, then accelerates again, timed to the container's own rhythm.
The second swing is aimed to cancel the first, exactly out of step with it.
Done correctly, the box arrives over the slot already hanging perfectly still.
Get the timing wrong, and the operator has to wait for the swing to die out on its own.
That wait can cost half a minute. Multiply it across two thousand containers and a ship misses its tide.
The hesitation was never caution. It is the fastest way to move thirty tons through open air.
